header.title: Frequently Asked Questions
header.subtitle: Here you can find answers about the algorithm, settings, usage, and the project.

disclaimer.title: What seating plans can achieve – and what they can't?
disclaimer.body: Klassenplan is a tool to support your teaching practice, not a replacement for it. Research shows that seating arrangements have a small but measurable effect on learning behavior.
disclaimer.researchNote: For context: reviews find effects that depend on the lesson’s goal – rows support focused individual work, especially for restless students, while clusters support exchange (Wannarka & Ruhl, 2008). The seating plan is one piece of the puzzle.
disclaimer.callToAction: The seating plans created by Klassenplan are starting points, not finished solutions. Your pedagogical assessment is decisive.

allgemein.title: General Questions
allgemein.description: Overview of algorithm, privacy, and offline usage.

algo_intro.q: What does the mixing algorithm actually do?
algo_intro.a: The algorithm distributes your class to all available seats based on weighted criteria. It starts with a heuristic initial placement and refines it in several passes. It takes into account preferred and distant partners, special needs, body heights, window/door preferences & more.

algo_neighbors.q: How does the algorithm evaluate neighbors?
algo_neighbors.intro: There are three gradations of neighborhoods that are weighted differently:
algo_neighbors.outro: These gradations help to represent free layouts as realistically as possible and to avoid conflicts in a targeted way.

no_account.q: Do I need an account or internet?
no_account.a: No. Klassenplan runs completely locally (IndexedDB + localStorage) and works offline after the first load. There is no login and no cloud synchronization. For device or browser switching, use the backup export/import.

imperfect.a: The algorithm evaluates table groups in the context of the entire room. A swap can help in one place but create bigger conflicts elsewhere. A perfect solution would have to check every combination and would not be practical. With its heuristic approach, Klassenplan achieves fast, comprehensible results that you can further refine via drag & drop.

gender_language.q: Why is the generic masculine form used?
gender_language.a: For reasons of readability and accessibility, the generic masculine is used. All genders are equally addressed.

klassenliste.title: Class list & class management
klassenliste.description: Multiple classes, CSV import, photos, attribute mode and the name game.

classes.a: Yes. The class switcher at the top left of the header lets you create as many classes as you like, rename them, switch between them or delete them. Each class keeps its own students, classroom layouts, seating plans and shuffle history. Deleting a class also removes its seating plans – so a backup beforehand is worth it.

csv.q: How do I import an existing class list?
csv.a: Use "Import class list" to upload a CSV file, the kind you can save from Excel, LibreOffice, Numbers or Google Sheets. A list from your school administration software – WebUntis, Schulmanager or SchILD, say – can usually be uploaded as it is: Klassenplan recognises the usual column names, reads accented characters correctly even when the file was saved on Windows, and skips a title line above the headers. The only requirement is a name column – "Name", "First name" or "Last name"; every other column such as gender, restless, window seat or preferred partner is optional, and unknown columns are simply ignored. Click "What the file looks like" to see an example, or download the CSV template and fill it in. If your file contains several name columns or several classes, Klassenplan asks what to import.

photos.q: Can I store photos of my students?
photos.a: Yes. Click a student in the class list; in the inspector on the right you add a photo through their portrait. The images are downscaled and stored exclusively on this device – they are never transferred. Using student photos requires consent from the school management, the students and their parents. Photos can be shown or hidden in the seating plan, in presentation mode and in the export, and they unlock the name game.

focusMode.q: How do I set an attribute for the whole class quickly?
focusMode.a: With attribute mode, under “View” in the toolbar. It asks everyone one question – “Who is restless?”, for instance – and you tap the students it applies to. Then it moves on to the next attribute until every yes/no attribute of the class is set.

bulk.q: How do I edit several students at once?
bulk.a: Tick several students in the list: the inspector on the right then sets gender, height, language level, social role or individual attributes for all of them at once. Search, filters and sorting above the list help you find the right students quickly.

demo.q: Can I try Klassenplan without real student data?
demo.a: Yes. As long as no class exists, load it from the empty class page with “Load sample class”; later you find the entry in the toolbar under “Import class list”. Klassenplan then creates a class of its own with 24 invented students, drawn portraits and a furnished classroom; your other classes stay untouched. If the sample class already exists, the same entry takes you to it. You can delete it at any time from the class switcher.

nameGame.a: The name game helps you learn the names of a new class. It only uses students with a photo and offers a photo quiz (find the name for a photo or the other way round; uncertain names come up more often) and a memory game of photo and name cards. Your progress stays locally on your device. You start it in the class toolbar under “Manage”.

eigenschaften.title: Student Properties & Criteria
eigenschaften.description: Overview of all properties and how the algorithm uses them.
eigenschaften.intro: On the class layer you record properties for every student – in the inspector, or for everyone at once in attribute mode. When you shuffle the seating plan, they come into play through the criteria. This overview shows every property, what it means and what the algorithm does with it.

gender.label: Gender
gender.description: Male, female or diverse – optional information.
gender.algorithm: Creates gender-mixed table groups when enabled.

height.label: Height
height.description: Small, Medium, or Tall – affects seating row.
height.algorithm: Places smaller students at the front and taller ones at the back for clear sightlines.

languageSkill.label: Language Skills
languageSkill.description: From native speaker to ESL support.
languageSkill.algorithm: Pairs language-strong students with beginners for mutual support.

performanceStrong.label: High Performer
performanceStrong.description: Currently showing particular strengths in class.
performanceStrong.algorithm: Enables heterogeneous (peer tutoring) or homogeneous grouping.

performanceWeak.label: Needs Support
performanceWeak.description: Currently showing additional support needs in class.
performanceWeak.algorithm: Enables targeted pairing with high-performing students.

needsFrontSeat.label: Front seat
needsFrontSeat.description: This student needs a front seat.
needsFrontSeat.algorithm: Places this student preferably in the front rows.

restless.label: Restless
restless.description: Currently showing restless behavior in class.
restless.algorithm: Separates students with restless behavior from each other.

shy.label: Shy
shy.description: Currently showing reserved behavior in class.
shy.algorithm: Places students with reserved behavior next to quieter classmates.

concentrationIssues.label: Easily Distracted
concentrationIssues.description: Currently showing concentration difficulties in class.
concentrationIssues.algorithm: Distributes students with concentration difficulties in the room and separates them from students with restless behavior.

socialRole.label: Social Role
socialRole.description: Mediator, Leader, Loner, or Social Hub.
socialRole.algorithm: Distributes social roles evenly across tables for balanced group dynamics.

wishPartner.label: Preferred Partner
wishPartner.description: Up to 3 prioritized partners the student wants to sit with.
wishPartner.algorithm: Places preferred partners at the same table, priority 1 counts more.

avoidPartner.label: Distance Request
avoidPartner.description: Up to 3 students to keep distance from.
avoidPartner.algorithm: Places these students at different tables.

prefersWindow.label: Window Seat
prefersWindow.description: Prefers a seat by the window.
prefersWindow.algorithm: Places the student closer to the window when possible.

prefersDoor.label: Near Door
prefersDoor.description: Prefers a seat near the door.
prefersDoor.algorithm: Places the student closer to the door when possible.

wunschpartner.title: Preferred & Distant Partners
wunschpartner.description: How preferred partners, distance wishes, and special needs influence the calculation.

relations.q: Where can I see all the wishes of the class at a glance?
relations.a: On the class layer under “View › Relationships”. It shows who would like to sit next to whom and who wants some distance, and marks the pairs who chose each other. Clicking a name opens that student in the inspector.

multi.q: How do multiple preferred and distant partners work?
multi.a: You can select up to 3 preferred and distant partners per student. The order determines the priority – the first selected partner is weighted more heavily than the third. The algorithm tries to fulfill as many wishes as possible, with Priority 1 taking precedence.

force.a: If the “Preferred Partners” criterion is set to “Consider” or higher, the algorithm seats pairs together unless other criteria weigh more heavily against it. At group tables (4/6), a seat at the same table counts as partially fulfilled.

needs.q: How does the system handle restless behavior, concentration difficulties, and distance wishes?
needs.a: Restlessness, distractibility and distance wishes each have a criterion of their own. Restless students are kept apart, easily distracted students are spread across the room, and distance wishes are respected as long as enough seats are available.

height.q: How does Klassenplan consider body heights and room preferences?
height.a: Body heights feed into the choice of seat so that smaller students sit as far forward as possible. Window and door preferences are stored per student and weighed against the windows and doors you placed in the room.

layout.title: Classroom & tables
layout.description: Tables and room elements, templates, distances and limits.

best.a: Let your creativity run free: you drag tables, windows, doors, the teacher’s desk, the blackboard and cabinets from the toolbar into the room and move them anywhere. “Set Up Classroom” builds a floor plan in one go, “Save Template” keeps it for other classes. The seating circle stays in sync with the table layout and can be adjusted separately.

measure.a: Seat positions are stored as pixel coordinates. Direct neighbors lie within the table width and height plus buffer; side and frontal neighbors may be slightly further away until they are no longer considered relevant.

limits.q: Are there limits on students and seats?
limits.a: Yes. Klassenplan is designed for a maximum of 36 students. In the room, the status bar shows whether there are seats for everyone and how many are missing.

settings.title: Criteria & fulfilment
settings.description: How you set the criteria and read how well a plan meets them.

recipes.intro: A recipe sets all criteria at once to suit the lesson. You find the recipes above the criteria:
recipes.outro: If you then change a single criterion, it becomes “Your own mix”. “Recommended mix” takes you back to the defaults at any time.

weights.q: What do Off, Consider, Important and Very important mean?
weights.intro: You set every criterion to one of four levels in the inspector to the right of the seating plan:
weights.outro: Criteria your class has no data for stay hidden and do not count.

check.q: How do I recognize that a mix meets the criteria?
check.a: On the seating plan, the inspector shows the fulfilment of the whole plan at the top and a bar with a percentage next to every criterion. Below, “Why this plan” explains in up to three sentences what the plan achieved and what remains open.

colors.q: What do the fulfilment colours mean?
colors.intro: The bars take their colour from how far a criterion is met:

interact.q: How do I find the seats a criterion affects?
interact.a: Move the mouse over a criterion’s bar: the seats it affects are marked in the seating plan. A click keeps the marking, a second click removes it. That way you quickly see where swapping seats by hand could improve the result.

percent.q: How are percentages calculated for multiple preferred partners?
percent.intro: Each preferred partner counts individually in the statistics:
percent.li2: At the same group table (4/6) = 50% fulfilled
percent.example: Example: 3 partners, 1 adjacent (100%) + 1 at table (50%) + 1 elsewhere (0%) = (100+50+0) / 3 = 50%

values.q: What do the individual statistics values indicate?
values.intro: Each criterion has its own degree of fulfillment, e.g.:
values.li1: Share of fulfilled wishes (direct partner or at table)
values.li2: Share of respected distance wishes (not at the same table)
values.li3: Share of new pairs (no repetition from previous plans)
values.li4: Share of affected students who are separated from each other
values.li5: Share of tables with balanced distribution

repeat.intro: The repetition evaluation considers both saved seating plans and the current mix history of the session:
repeat.li1: Pairs from older plans receive decreasing weight (newer ones count more)
repeat.li2: The last mixes are weighted more heavily so that pairs do not repeat immediately
repeat.outro: This avoids the same students sitting next to each other constantly when you shuffle several times in a row. Not every shuffle is actually put into practice, though – and that is exactly where the mix history on its own reaches its limits.
repeat.usageIntro: Klassenplan therefore keeps track of which seating charts were really in use. There is nothing to tick – what counts is what you do anyway:
repeat.usage1: Showing a seating chart in presentation mode
repeat.usage2: Printing a seating chart or exporting it as PDF, PNG or SVG
repeat.usage3: Saving a seating chart under a name you chose yourself
repeat.usageOutro: Only the seating neighbourhoods and a timestamp are stored, entirely on your own device – no cloud, no analytics service. On the first strong signal a short notice asks: if it really was just a test, one click takes the chart back out of the count.
repeat.weightNote: For repeat avoidance these real seating charts are read first; mixes from the running session now weigh only half as much. A long session of trying things out can no longer drown out the result.
repeat.viewNote: In the seating plan’s toolbar, “Neighbourhoods” shows who has sat next to whom and how often – including the data it rests on, from which you can remove individual plans.

tipps.title: Tips for unwanted results
tipps.description: What you can do if a mix doesn't convince immediately.

improve.q: How can I improve the result?
improve.intro: Use a combination of the following strategies:
improve.li1: Set the criteria that matter to “Important” or “Very important” – or pick a fitting recipe
improve.li2: Mix multiple times to use different random starts
improve.li3: Adjust individual seats manually via drag & drop and lock them if necessary so that the algorithm no longer changes them.
improve.li4: Take back a poor shuffle with Ctrl/Cmd+Z or load an earlier result under “Saved Plans”

unterricht.title: Presenting, exporting & tools
unterricht.description: Projector, seating circle, printing and the three classroom tools.

present.a: “Present” in the middle of the status bar shows the seating plan or circle large on the projector or smartboard. Every control sits in one bar below the plan: teacher or student view (which turns the plan to the class’s point of view), plan or circle, photos, colours, room elements, a contrast mode for bright rooms and the size. The wall shows first names, whatever the editor shows. In fullscreen (key F) the bar disappears and comes back as soon as you move the mouse to the bottom edge.

tools.q: What are “Who’s next?”, “Where does who sit?” and “Build groups”?
tools.a: Three tools for the lesson, each a page of its own that works standing up on a tablet or phone. “Who’s next?” draws a random student, and everyone gets a turn before anyone comes up twice. “Where does who sit?” finds a student in the room. “Build groups” draws groups from the class and keeps distance wishes apart where it can. You open them in the seating plan’s toolbar under “Tools”, “Build groups” also from presentation mode. Nothing is stored.

circle.q: How does the seating circle mode work?
circle.a: On the seating plan, choose “Circle” under “Arrangement” in the toolbar. Klassenplan calculates a suitable circle automatically and links it to your current seating plan. You can adjust the seats in the circle by drag & drop without changing the seating plan, and present or export it separately.

exportFormats.q: In which formats can I export the seating plan?
exportFormats.a: The export page saves PDF, PNG and SVG and prints directly – handy for letters to parents, cover folders or the school portal. You choose the seating plan or the circle under “Arrangement” in the toolbar, each in portrait or landscape.

print.q: I want to print the seating plan and have the blackboard shown at the bottom as orientation. Is that possible?
print.a: Yes. On the export page, set the orientation to “Portrait” under “Page Format” on the right and leave the blackboard switched on under “Room Elements”. If your desk is at the back of the room, set the viewing direction to “From the back”: the plan turns by 180° and the names stay readable. That way the printout keeps the same orientation as the classroom.

names.q: The names on the plan are too long – what can I do?
names.a: On the seating plan under “Show in the plan › Names”, in presentation mode and under “Names” on the export page you decide how names appear: first name only, first name + last initial, or first and last name. Names that would look the same are told apart automatically – “Frida Ehrmann” and “Frida Emmerich” become “Frida Eh.” and “Frida Em.”.

oberflaeche.title: Operation & interface
oberflaeche.description: Dark mode, shortcuts, undo, the tour, tablets and installation.

undo.a: Yes, on all three layers: in the class list, in the room and in the seating plan and circle – so a student deleted by accident comes back with their photo, for example. The arrows at the bottom left of the status bar undo and redo changes, and so do Ctrl/Cmd + Z and Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Z.

shortcuts.a: Plenty – Ctrl/Cmd + C, V and X copy, paste and cut tables, for example, and Ctrl/Cmd + B folds the toolbar in and out. The question mark at the top right lists every shortcut of the current layer under “Shortcuts”; the ? key opens it directly.

tour.q: Is there an introduction to using Klassenplan?
tour.a: Yes. On your first visit, a short tour shows you the most important places on every layer – from the class switcher and the toolbar to the criteria and the seating circle. The tour never blocks anything: you can keep working, close it with Escape or switch it off for good with “Don’t show again”. The question mark at the top right restarts the tour of the current layer at any time – and leads to these questions, too.

dark.a: Yes. In the app, switch between the light and dark colour scheme with the gear at the top right; on the information pages, with the switch in the footer. Your choice is stored locally in the browser and loaded automatically on your next visit.

tablet.q: Can I use Klassenplan on a tablet or whiteboard?
tablet.a: Yes. The interface is built for touch, long press for context menus included, and runs smoothly on tablets and whiteboards. On a phone, the three tools “Who’s next?”, “Where does who sit?” and “Build groups” are meant for the lesson; class and room are better set up on a larger screen.

pwa.q: Can I install Klassenplan like an app?
pwa.a: Yes! Klassenplan is a Progressive Web App (PWA) and can be installed directly on your device. In Chrome, Edge, or Safari, look for "Add to Home Screen" or "Install App" in the browser menu. After that, Klassenplan launches like a standalone app from the dock or start menu – faster, with its own icon, and without the browser bar.

backups.title: Backups & Persistence
backups.description: How data is stored locally, how backups work and how to move to a new device.

where.a: All data is stored in the browser (IndexedDB for core data, localStorage for settings). There is no cloud, no account, and no server synchronization. Your data stays on your device and is not accessible from outside.

loss.intro: Yes, and that is the price of nothing ever leaving your device. Everything sits in your browser's storage, and browsers clear that out under certain conditions:
loss.li1: Safari, for example, deletes the data of sites you have not visited for seven days.
loss.li2: “Clear browsing data”, “remove website data” or resetting the browser wipe it too.
loss.li3: In a private or incognito window it is gone as soon as you close the window.
loss.outro: Klassenplan asks the browser for persistent storage the first time you create a class, which lowers the risk considerably — but no browser guarantees it. A backup is the only copy that does not depend on any of this. It is safest kept off the machine, on a USB stick or in your school's cloud storage.

how.a: The export creates a file encrypted with your password (at least 8 characters) containing all classes, students including their photos, seating plans, shuffle and usage history, seating circle, classroom features, templates and settings. Without that password the file cannot be restored – so keep it safe to avoid losing your data.

deviceChange.q: How do I move my classes to a new computer?
deviceChange.intro: Through the backup file — there is no sync between devices, because there is no server.
deviceChange.li1: On the old device, click “Backup” in the toolbar of the class layer, choose “Export backup” and set a password.
deviceChange.li2: Get the file onto the new device, for example via USB stick, a cloud folder or an email to yourself.
deviceChange.li3: On the new device, open Klassenplan and choose “Import backup” under “Backup” in the toolbar.
deviceChange.li4: Pick the file, enter the password and confirm “Replace everything”.
deviceChange.outro: Your classes, students including photos, seating plans and templates are then on the new device. The file works on any operating system and in any browser. Without the password, however, it cannot be opened.

frequency.q: How often should I make a backup?
frequency.a: For example after creating a class or after setting up and saving a classroom. Klassenplan reminds you on its own once your last backup is more than 30 days old. You can postpone that reminder or switch it off for good via “Stop reminding me”.

update.q: What happens to my backup after a Klassenplan update?
update.a: Backups are backward compatible and are meant to stay that way – should that ever change, I will provide an extended migration tool. New versions automatically migrate older backups. After major changes, it is worth creating a fresh export so that you have secured the latest structure.

restore.q: What happens when I import a backup?
restore.a: You choose between "Replace everything" and "Merge". Replacing overwrites existing students, seating plans and templates with the backup – this cannot be undone. Merging adds students and seating plans from the backup to the existing ones; the classroom and settings then come from the backup.

projekt.title: Project & Support
projekt.description: Information on costs, updates, and how you can contribute.

cost.a: No, Klassenplan is a free tool that I work on in my free time. I originally developed Klassenplan for my own needs (with the help of Claude Code) and I am happy if it helps you and you like using it. If you like Klassenplan and would like to support its hosting costs as well as further development, I would be happy about a donation via PayPal. You can find all info under “Support” – in the app at the very bottom of every toolbar. Thank you!

update.a: When a new version is available, Klassenplan asks whether to load it – your data stays as it is. With the gear at the top right you can also look for updates yourself. What has changed is listed in the changelog.

feedback.q: How can I give feedback or participate?
feedback.a: You can send a message at any time via the feedback page. I look forward to practical experiences, bug reports, and feature ideas.
feedback.openSource: Klassenplan is open source: you can view the source code, report bugs, or contribute your own changes.

license.q: Under which license is Klassenplan released?
license.a: The source code is licensed under the GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 (AGPL-3.0-or-later). You are free to use, modify, and redistribute Klassenplan – including your own customized versions – as long as you release them under the same terms and disclose the source code. If you run a modified version on a server, its users must be able to access the corresponding source code.
